newsitem.title: INDIA: India says May export rebound "encouraging".
newsitem.headline: India says May export rebound "encouraging".

text.p: Indian exports rose in May for the first time in three months, the government announced on Wednesday, describing the rebound as an encouraging sign in a largely grim economic picture.
Merchandise exports stood at $2.86 billion in May, up from $2.52 billion in April and $2.63 billion in May 1996, the government said.
The Commerce Ministry said May's growth was "encouraging and may indicate export optimism".
Preliminary data showed growth in exports of spices, leather manufactures, marine products, engineering goods, electronic goods, textiles and handicrafts.

The slowdown in exports had worried policymakers, and on Tuesday Commerce Minister Bola Bulli Ramaiah said he was frustrated with the value of the rupee which exporters claim is too strong and prices their products out of the world market.
"I am not happy but I have to see the overall situation," Ramaiah said.
The Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India on Wednesday urged the government to allow the rupee to depreciate gradually against the U.S. dollar.

"Export stagnation is something that India cannot afford and the liberal import policy has to be coupled with growth in exports," Ramaiah said on Wednesday, referring to progressive reductions in India's import duties over the past six years.
Exports grew only four percent to $33.1 billion in the 1996/97 fiscal year that ended on March 31, compared with a 21.4 percent growth rate in 1995/96.
Imports grew six percent in 1996/97 to $38.5 billion, far slower than the 19.2 percent expansion in 1995/96. In May, imports fell 1.4 percent to $3.2 billion.

The slowdown in trade has mirrored weakness in the industrial sector. Industry expanded by 6.7 percent in 1996/97, compared with an 11.6 percent jump in the previous fiscal year. In March, the growth rate slowed to 2.9 percent.

Bidisha Ganguly of W.I. Carr Securities in Bombay said May's trade figures were "not too bad". She noted that imports had surged 19 percent in May 1996, meaning the drop in May 1997 was from a high level.
But she said the increase in exports in May may have been somewhat inflated as many shipments that normally would have been made in April were delayed because of an 11-day truckers' strike.
